Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Loaded. Here's my design plan before I build.

**Color** — a records-office palette, cool not warm: paper `#EDF0F3`, blue-black ink `#131A21`, blue-biased grey `#4A5763` (chosen, not default mid-grey), and — the key device — a single-hue *ramp* encoding proof strength, pale slate `#9FB3C0` → `#5B8CA8` → `#1F6F8B` → deep `#0B4A63`. Ochre `#A8641A` for today's broken rule, brick `#97302B` for failures.

**Type** — Iowan Old Style for display (real character, on your Mac, not Georgia-default), system humanist sans for body, SF Mono for the identifiers and SQL. No webfont links, since the CSP would silently fall back.

**Layout** — one narrow reading column with full-bleed specimen blocks breaking out. The hero is the ladder itself with the threshold line drawn across it: that single graphic *is* the idea.

entity_identities · design note · 30 Jul 2026

Uniqueness should depend on how well a claim is proven.

Not on what kind of identifier it is. That one shift is all “assurance‑gated uniqueness” means — and your code already has every piece it needs.

Start here — the sentence version

Right now your database enforces one rule for everything: no two entities may claim the same string. A GitHub user ID and a phone number scribbled into an address book are held to identical standards.

The proposal is to make that rule apply only to claims that are actually proven. Everything weaker still gets stored and still helps match people — it just loses the power to block or overwrite.

That's it. “Assurance” is the word your codebase already uses for how strongly something is vouched for. “Gated” means the uniqueness rule sits behind a trust threshold instead of applying to all rows.

The rule you have today

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_entity_identities_live_unique
  ON entity_identities (organization_id, namespace, identifier)
  WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

One rule, every namespace, comparing the literal characters of identifier. It fails in two directions at once, and your four remaining merge approvals are living proof of both.

Two spellings of one number never collide.

winner  05324764881  (typed into an address book)
loser   905324764881  (from WhatsApp)

Today

Different strings, so no conflict. Both rows are stored happily and the duplicate person survives. Nothing notices.

With the change

Still doesn't collide — but the weak claim is now stored as evidence, so the matching rules can see it and say so plainly.

And when it does collide, it deletes the proof.

both sides  905067888845  (identical spelling)

Today — the real bug

The second write hits the index and is silently skipped. No error, no log entry anyone reads. The one fact that proved these were the same person is now recorded on only one side — so matching can't see it either.

With the change

A collision between two proven claims is a real event. It surfaces: either the write is rejected naming the entity that already holds it, or it raises a merge for review. Never silence.

What your code already knows

Every fact a connector produces already carries a strength rating, on a four-step scale with a total order and a helper called assuranceMeets that your matching rules already consult. Then it reaches storage and gets thrown away.

Here is that ladder, weakest to strongest, and where a threshold would sit:

self_attestedSomeone typed it in
your 534 address-book phones
Evidence only
↑ below the line: helps match, never blocks  ·  ↓ above: enforces uniqueness
cookie_sessionRead from a logged-in session
linkedin_slug, ig_username
Enforces
oauth_verifiedThe provider vouched for it
auth_user_id, github_user_id
Enforces
oauth_verified_admin_roleVouched, with admin scope
workspace-admin grants
Enforces

Where the line sits is the decision I need from you. I put it at cookie_session here on purpose: that keeps today's behaviour for all ~7,200 provider-sourced rows and changes it only for hand-entered ones. In my last message I said oauth_verified, which on reflection is worse — it would quietly drop enforcement for the 3,600-odd rows that come from your browser extension.

Why not just delete the phone and email rows?

It was a fair option, and it's simpler. But it buys safety by giving up deterministic de-duplication completely — every duplicate becomes a human decision forever.

Gating on strength gives you the same safety for weak data, because weak data never enforces anything, while keeping the win when a number really is verified. It strictly dominates deletion.

And the opposite half-measure — adding canonical comparison without the strength gate — would be worse than today: a shared family phone typed into two contacts would suddenly hard-collide, and one of two real people would lose their record.

What actually changes in your workspace

7,200provider-ID rows — behaviour unchanged
462phone + email rows — gain a strength rating
1,069metadata identifiers that could safely become evidence
4merge approvals that stay manual regardless

The 1,069 figure is the pleasant surprise. Converting those loose metadata strings into stored claims looked risky when every claim enforced uniqueness — it threatened to mint a huge approval queue. Once weak claims enforce nothing, that conversion is safe: they simply become structured, traceable evidence for rules you already run.

And the honest limit: your four stragglers stay manual. A hand-typed 05324764881 and a verified 905324764881 cannot be matched without someone knowing the number is Turkish. This design refuses to guess a country code — which is the correct call, and means those four remain a human judgement.

One nuance, so the name makes full sense

Strength is a floor, per claim. There's also a ceiling, per namespace: your registry already declares uniquePerOrg, and marks email_domain false because many people share a domain. Some namespaces can never be unique no matter how well proven.

So the finished rule reads: enforce uniqueness when the namespace permits it and the claim is proven enough to earn it. Two knobs, both of which already exist in your code. uniquePerOrg is declared but nothing reads it

Every count and code reference here was read from live production or origin/main, not from memory. The assurance, normalized_value and valid_to columns do not exist yet — which namespace lands at which strength is a decision to make, not data to read.

**https://claude.ai/code/artifact/74b06027-1fc7-4ece-9a65-d40a9d6d417f**

The whole idea in one sentence: **today your database holds a GitHub user ID and a phone number scribbled into an address book to exactly the same standard.** One rule, every row — no two entities may claim the same string.

"Assurance" is just the word your own codebase already uses for how strongly something is vouched for. `AssuranceLevel` is a four-step scale with a total order and an `assuranceMeets` helper your matching rules already call. "Gated" means the uniqueness rule sits behind a threshold on that scale instead of applying to everything. Proven claims enforce uniqueness. Weak ones still get stored and still help match people — they just can't block or overwrite anything.

The page walks it through your actual data: the ladder with the threshold drawn across it, then the two ways today's rule fails, side by side with what changes.

Two things in there worth flagging directly.

**I moved the threshold and it matters.** Last message I said `oauth_verified`. On reflection that's the wrong line — it would quietly drop enforcement for the ~3,600 rows that come from your browser extension (`linkedin_slug`, `ig_username`), which work fine today. At `cookie_session` the behaviour of all ~7,200 provider-ID rows is untouched and only hand-entered values change. That's the minimal-change version and where I'd put it.

**The second failure mode is the one to look at.** When the index *does* fire — identical spellings on both sides — the write is silently skipped. So the single fact that proved two records were the same person ends up recorded on one side only, which means matching can't see it either. The constraint deletes its own evidence. That's a bug independent of this whole design, and it's the piece I'd fix first regardless of what you decide.

Confidence: high on the diagnosis and the numbers — all read from live prod or `origin/main`. Medium on the design, which nobody but me has reviewed. The `assurance` / `normalized_value` / `valid_to` columns don't exist yet, so which namespace lands at which strength is a decision, not data I can look up.

- Or I take the silent-skip fix as a standalone PR now — it's a correctness bug whichever way this goes.
- If you'd rather kill the idea: say so and I'll do the simple version instead, adding the identity write parameter to `manage_entity` and leaving uniqueness exactly as it is.

aiTitle: Fix user merge entity policy error

content.text:
Settled, and it means I was over-engineering. Decisive evidence:

```ts
type ResolutionDecision = "auto_merge" | "review";

const DEFAULT_PERSON_RESOLUTION_RULES = [
  { fields: ["email"], normalizer: "email", onMatch: "review" },
  { fields: ["phone"], normalizer: "phone", onMatch: "review" },
];
```

Every default person rule is **`review`**. `auto_merge` exists, but contact identifiers deliberately don't use it — because a shared phone isn't proof.

That kills my assurance-gated design. I was building a uniqueness mechanism to prevent duplicates, when the shipped policy explicitly declines to auto-merge on phone or email regardless. No amount of canonical-value or assurance machinery would have prevented those 18 reviews — the policy asks for them on purpose. **Your 18 approvals were the system working as designed.** The bug was only ever the fingerprint, which we fixed.

So the real defect list is much shorter than anything I've pitched:

**One real bug.** The silent skip — a contested claim vanishes with no signal, destroying the evidence that proved sameness.

**One real gap, and it's an asymmetry.** The connector path (`entity-link-upsert`) looks up existing entities by identity before creating — that's what "upsert" means. `createEntity`, which `run_sdk` and `manage_entity` use, does `INSERT INTO entities` unconditionally with a slug from the name. No lookup, no `ON CONFLICT`. One path resolves, the other creates blind.

**And nothing else.** No assurance column, no canonical column, no index change, no `uniquePerOrg` wiring, no migration, no backfill. The scalable answer is that the *policy* is already the knob: if you ever want verified matches to fuse automatically, you set `onMatch: auto_merge` in `x-lobu-resolution` — configuration, not a schema change.

Two PRs, stated in one sentence each: make contested claims surface instead of vanishing, and make `createEntity` consult the resolver the connector path already uses. Let me start with the bug.

<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. If other harnesses like pi or codex need it, modify AGENTS.md -->

@AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source is in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- Main packages: `core` shared types/utils, `plugin-api` native plugin contracts, `plugin-host` deterministic plugin composition, `server` gateway + embedded runtime, `agent-worker` Lobu agent execution, `connectors` built-in connectors, `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Before editing a package, read its nearest `AGENTS.md` if present.
- `docs/GOTCHAS.md` collects the mechanical traps (build, SQL, testing, submodule, browser) that have each cost a debugging session. Skim the section for the surface you are touching before you start, and grep it when something looks inexplicable.

## Hard invariants
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly — work in a worktree.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout.
- One branch = one concern (not one file). Tangential task → commit/push/open current work, then branch fresh from `main`. Split only for genuinely independent concerns or an unreviewable diff.
- **Multi-replica correctness is mandatory.** Never put shared required state in an in-memory Map/singleton another replica must read or mutate. If a feature relies on cross-pod visibility, use Postgres-mediated state/signal.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone/supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are frequently real human signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Workers never receive real credentials.** They may receive only placeholders/proxied access. The only exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived credential leases (see `packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one of them.
- Default to static `import`. New dynamic imports require measured cost justification here or in the package AGENTS plus a rationale comment at the call site. Tests may dynamically import after mocks.
  - Node-version gate exceptions: `packages/cli/bin/lobu.js` defers the existing CLI graph without duplicating it, and `packages/server/src/server-entry.ts` adds an 842-byte gate in front of the 4.34 MB server graph (measured 2026-07-24). Both call sites must stay dependency-free until their checks pass.
- Bug fixes require red→fix→green evidence, with both outputs pasted into the PR body. If you cannot reproduce, stop and report the dead end — do not ship a speculative fix.
- Never report done off a green typecheck. Boot it, exercise every branch you touched, clean up test data. If "compiles" is all you ran, say so explicitly.
- Gates are non-negotiable (sequence in "Ship a change" below). `make pre-pr` builds first — that build step is what protects against a stale-dist false green. `make review` is an LLM verdict only: it does NOT run typecheck/knip/tests and is not proof CI will pass.
- The agent-facing product name is **Behavior**; `watcher` is internal engine/DB vocabulary. It must not appear in MCP tool schemas/names/descriptions, ClientSDK discovery metadata, or the connector-sdk public reaction contract — `make pre-pr` fails on it. Internal identifiers (`actingWatcherId`, table/column names, comments) are fine.
- `make review-fix` is the unposted fixer pass and runs BEFORE the first `make review`; verify its diff and commit it. Never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop — each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other instance and fix in one pass — a diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one. Same root cause twice = stop reviewing, grep-enumerate. A class-wide fix is in scope for the branch that found it and does not count as scope creep.
- **Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state.** When a durable coordination or delivery operation fails, its caller must not reinterpret the error as proceed/deliver/skip. Propagate a retry, defer, or terminal-failure outcome with a visible log; if the operation may already have succeeded, reconcile idempotently before retrying. Treat lock timeouts, pool errors, and ambiguous or expired rows as failures, not as "nothing changed."
- **Coordination design brake.** A change that needs a second lock, a second retry/deferral budget, or a prose termination argument to explain why it halts is patching a misplaced check — stop and re-derive where the decision belongs before adding mechanism. Find the chokepoint that already serializes the action (e.g. worker dispatch is serialized by `job-router` on the worker-SSE-owner pod) and put the check there; prefer deleting the state transition over coordinating it, and reuse queue-native retry over hand-rolled hold/requeue.
- **Stage by explicit path; never commit the whole tree of a worktree that hosted other work.** A commit is a snapshot — stale file copies silently revert already-merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal the task's intended file list; extra files = stop. Verify a "reverts merged work" review finding by diff direction against `origin/main`, never dismiss it as merge-base noise.

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce the bug (red) before fixing it. Fix, then prove green.
3. Test: `make test-unit` (no DB) / `make test-integration` (needs `DATABASE_URL` with pgvector). One file: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites.
4. `make pre-pr` — build, typecheck, knip, lint, exposed-surface naming.
5. `make review-fix` on the settled diff and verify what it changed — it edits the working tree, so re-read the files before trusting them.
6. Stage by explicit path (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`), commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list. Extra files = stop.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title, e.g. `fix(server): …`).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD. It posts the `pi-review` status, which is a REQUIRED check.
9. Merge squash once CI is green: `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin`. Never `--admin` past a check that has not reported.
10. Prod-visible surface? Verify it live after rollout. Set a self-rescheduling `ScheduleWakeup` (~1500s) carrying the rollout gate: poll the deployed SHA, then `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"` with `MERGE_SHA=$(gh pr view <n> --json mergeCommit --jq .mergeCommit.oid)`. Two ways this gate silently never opens — **gate on the squash commit, not your branch head** (a squash merge writes a new commit with no ancestry link to the branch, so the branch head exits 1 forever: PR #2280 has identical trees and still fails), and **keep that argument order** (merge commit first; reversed, it accepts a stale deploy). Run the live check when it lands, and write the result back to memory.

## Agent workflow
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create. Do not create `*.md` unless asked.
- Prefer `bun`; do not use npm/yarn/pnpm for repo work.
- Fix unused params by deleting them, not `_`-prefixing.
- Never `git stash`; use WIP commits and squash later.
- Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI (it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work). Rebase locally against `origin/main`, then diff against the last real feature commit before squashing — except on submodule-pointer branches, where you must `git merge` (see `docs/GOTCHAS.md`, "Submodule & cross-repo").
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- Show the diff, not a summary. Before claiming done — on your own work or a dispatched agent's — surface `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`. An agent's self-report is a claim; the diff is the evidence.
- UI PRs owe before/after screenshots, and `gh` cannot upload images inline. Capture before shots from the unmodified branch and after shots from the same booted app (auth recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`), base64-embed the PNGs into one self-contained HTML comparison page, publish it as a claude.ai artifact, and link it from the PR.
- Any subagent with write access (Edit/Write/Bash) runs in its own worktree; only grep/read agents share the parent. Two writing agents must NEVER share a worktree — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work.
- Dispatch code-writing agents through `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` and brief them with the absolute `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/` path. Only task-setup does the submodule branch pinning, post-init `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation.
- Do repetitive multi-file edits (renames, signature changes, import rewrites) inline or with one script. Reserve subagents for read-only breadth or genuinely isolated parallel work.
- Before adding an env var, grep for the one the codebase already reads. Do not rename existing vars to a "cleaner" convention unasked.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence (dangling import, completed migration, superseded impl). Low prod usage is not a delete signal; trace the workflow, not just the import graph — docs and help text are load-bearing too.
- **Absence is never proven by a grep on a working tree.** To prove code does *not* exist, run `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main` — the fetch is load-bearing, `origin/main` itself goes stale. Applies to every existence check, including the deletion-evidence rule above.
- Slack link pasted (`slack.com/archives/…?thread_ts=`) → run `scripts/slack-thread-viewer.js "<link>"` first.
- To drive the user's real logged-in browser, use the paired Owletto extension — recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`. Do **not** assume CDP/browser-auth is required.
- Unsure in planning → ask before making conflicting or irreversible choices. Mid-execution, block on a question only for irreversible/destructive actions or decisions that are genuinely the user's; for reversible choices with a clear recommended option, take it and flag the choice in your summary.

## Session efficiency
- Never poll in the foreground (`sleep`/`until`/`while` wait loops, repeated `tail`). Run long waits (dev-server boot, CI, deploys) in the background and act on the completion notification.
- Prefer DOM reads (`get_page_text`, `read_page`, `javascript_tool`) over screenshots; screenshot only when visual layout itself is under test. Screenshots are the #1 context-bloat source.
- Read a file before editing it, and re-read it after any external change (a fixer pass, another agent, a rebase). Blind edits fail and cost a retry round-trip.
- Read PR status compactly: `gh pr view <n> --json number,title,isDraft,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision` plus `gh pr checks <n> --required`. Never `--json statusCheckRollup` — measured on PR 2280 it is 7520 bytes against 861, 8.7x larger and less legible.
- Batch narrow fixes into one commit, verified once at the end of the batch — not per fix. It never justifies skipping a reproducer or a correctness-critical test. For a one-line or config-only change, take one CI snapshot and move on.

Verify a "reverts merged work" review finding by diff direction against `origin/main`, never dismiss it as merge-base noise.

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce the bug (red) before fixing it. Fix, then prove green.
3. Test: `make test-unit` (no DB) / `make test-integration` (needs `DATABASE_URL` with pgvector). One file: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites.
4. `make pre-pr` — build, typecheck, knip, lint, exposed-surface naming.
5. `make review-fix` on the settled diff and verify what it changed — it edits the working tree, so re-read the files before trusting them.
6. Stage by explicit path (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`), commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list. Extra files = stop.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title, e.g. `fix(server): …`).

9. Merge squash once CI is green: `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin`. Never `--admin` past a check that has not reported.
10. Prod-visible surface? Verify it live after rollout. - Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create. Do not create `*.md` unless asked.
- Prefer `bun`; do not use npm/yarn/pnpm for repo work.
- Fix unused params by deleting them, not `_`-prefixing.
- Never `git stash`; use WIP commits and squash later.

content.text:
Good catch, and you're right to flag it — my `attachEntityIdentities` added a **second query** to the connector ingestion hot path, and worse, it fires in the most common case.

The steady state for a repeat message from a known sender is: the claim already exists on that entity with a `connection_id` set, so the `DO UPDATE` predicate doesn't match, so the row isn't returned — and my code then ran a follow-up `SELECT` to ask "is this mine or contested?" on every single message.

And it's unnecessary, because **the caller already knows.** `lookupMatches` runs earlier in the flow and returns the owner of every identifier; the original code at line 811 already reconciles against that map. Contested is derivable from data in hand, with zero extra queries.

I also shouldn't have been tempted to widen the `DO UPDATE` predicate to force rows to return — that predicate (`connection_id IS NULL AND EXCLUDED.connection_id IS NOT NULL`) exists to avoid writing a new row version per message. Widening it would add WAL and table bloat to every repeat sender.

So: the writer inserts and returns what attached, exactly as before; each caller derives contested from the ownership map it already holds. Same single query on the hot path, and the fail-closed error propagation costs nothing.

content.text:
`review-fix` is running in the background (it edits the working tree, so I won't touch files until it lands).

**On your hot-path question — the answer changed the design, and thank you for asking it.** My first cut had `attachEntityIdentities` doing an INSERT and then a follow-up `SELECT` to classify each claim as mine-vs-contested. That second query would have fired on the *most common* ingestion case: a repeat message from a known sender, where the claim already exists with its provenance filled, so it doesn't match the `DO UPDATE` predicate and doesn't come back. Every inbound message would have paid for it.

Two ways out, one of them a trap. Widening the `DO UPDATE` predicate so those rows always return would work — and would write a new row version per message, adding WAL and table bloat to the hottest path. That predicate is there on purpose.

The real answer is that no query was needed. `lookupMatches` already runs earlier and returns the owner of every identifier; the original code at line 811 already reconciles against it. So contested is derivable from data in hand. The writer is now one statement, and `contestedAgainst` is a pure function over the map the caller already has.

Net effect on ingestion: **identical query count to before.** One lookup, one insert. What's new is that a failed identity write now propagates instead of being swallowed into `[]` — which costs nothing and stops a DB error from reading as "this entity has no identities," the state that lets the next writer mint a duplicate.

Where I did accept a cost is the tool path: `manage_entity create` with identities now does one extra `SELECT` before inserting. That's an agent-facing call, not per-message ingestion, and it's the whole point of the change.

**Committed so far** — six files, typecheck clean, `pre-pr` green:

```
packages/core/.../manage-entity.ts              identities input + attached_to_existing
packages/server/.../identity-lookup.ts          NEW — lookup, writer, pure resolvers
packages/server/.../identity-lookup.test.ts     NEW — 10 unit tests
packages/server/.../manage_entity.ts            resolve-before-create at the tool boundary
packages/server/.../entity-link-upsert.ts       delegates; errors propagate; contested logged
packages/server/.../manage-entity-identities.test.ts  NEW — 7 integration tests
```

Tests: 10 unit + 7 integration green. Mutation-verified twice — disabling the attach branch fails the dedupe test; bypassing normalization fails three, including the one asserting an unparseable phone never becomes a claim.

The integration test that matters reproduces your prod shape directly: create "Esref" with `905322356586`, then create "Esref Kaya" with `+90 (532) 235 65 86`, and assert one person exists with `attached_to_existing: true`. There's also a test pinning that `05324764881` does **not** match `905324764881`, so the no-country-code-guessing rule can't be quietly regressed.

I'll pick up when `review-fix` reports, verify its diff, then push and run `make review` once before merging.

content.text:
The affected suites are running in the background. Where things stand:

**`review-fix` found two real gaps in my code, both worth having:**

The important one: **the deferred-approval path dropped the identities entirely.** When an agent's create is held for approval, my version computed the claims and then returned early — so when a human later approved, `createEntity` ran with no identities and would have minted exactly the duplicate this PR exists to prevent. The fix threads `identity_claims` and `identity_source_connector` through `buildCreateDeferral` → `proposeEntityCreate` so they survive in `runs.action_input`.

Second: it **wired up `uniquePerOrg`** — the field I'd found declared-but-inert. `normalizeRequestedIdentities` now drops generic namespaces that aren't unique per org, so `email_domain` can't be submitted as an identity claim. That's the narrow, justified version of making it load-bearing, and it moved into `identity-lookup.ts` with its own unit tests.

**Two things I had to correct in its work.** Its new deferral test never actually deferred — `approval_queued` came back undefined because nothing seeded a policy holding creates for approval, so it was asserting against a path it wasn't exercising. Seeding a `write_approval_policies` row with `create → approval` makes it real; 8/8 now pass.

And `make review-fix` itself was **SIGTERM'd mid-run** (`Terminated: 15`), same as `make review` earlier today, so I treated the tree as suspect rather than trusting the exit code — typecheck clean at 0 errors, and I read every hunk in the three files it touched that I hadn't.

**One change I pushed back on and kept anyway.** It added a compensating `DELETE FROM entities` when the now-fail-closed identity write rejects. I'd normally reach for a transaction instead of hand-rolled compensation, but the slug-retry loop above it depends on surviving a failed `INSERT`, and an aborted transaction can't do that. A hard delete is defensible here since nothing references the row yet. I documented why a transaction isn't available and noted the partial-insert caveat where the FK holds the delete back.

Confidence: high on the mechanism — typecheck clean, 21 tests green, and two mutations caught earlier (disabling the attach branch fails the dedupe test; bypassing normalization fails three). Not yet verified: the wider connector suite currently running, and I haven't mutation-tested the new deferral path.

I'll report when the suites land, then push and run `make review` once.

## What

`manage_entity(action='create')` now accepts identity claims and resolves them **before** inserting, so it attaches to an entity that already claims the identifier instead of minting a duplicate.

The connector path (`entity-link-upsert`) has always looked up owners first — that is what "upsert" means there. The tool path, used by `run_sdk` and agents, did `INSERT INTO entities` unconditionally with a slug derived from the name. That asymmetry is how an address-book import created a second person for contacts a connector already knew, producing merge approvals a human then had to clear.

## Why not a schema change

Considered and rejected: adding a canonical-value column, an `assurance` column, or moving the uniqueness index. None would have prevented those duplicates — `DEFAULT_PERSON_RESOLUTION_RULES` sets `onMatch: "review"` for both email and phone, so the policy deliberately declines to auto-merge on contact identifiers. The gap was never uniqueness enforcement; it was that one write path never looked. `onMatch` in `x-lobu-resolution` remains the knob if auto-merge is ever wanted — configuration, not a migration.

## Behaviour

- One existing owner → that entity is used, `attached_to_existing: true`.
- No owner → normal create, then claims attached.
- Two *different* existing entities claiming different identifiers in one call → refused with 409 naming the candidates. Picking either would silently fuse two real records.
- A value its namespace cannot normalize is ignored rather than stored as a claim.
- Generic namespaces that are not unique per org (`email_domain`) are rejected as claims. This makes the previously **declared-but-inert** `uniquePerOrg` field load-bearing for the first time.

## Hot path

`attachEntityIdentities` is deliberately one statement with no follow-up read. A first draft classified each claim as mine-vs-contested with a second `SELECT`, which would have fired on the most common ingestion case (repeat message from a known sender, where the row exists with provenance filled and so does not match the `DO UPDATE` predicate). Widening that predicate to force rows to return was also rejected — it writes a new row version per message. Contested claims are instead derived from the ownership map `lookupMatches` already fetched, via a pure function. **Query count on ingestion is unchanged.**

## Fail-closed

`insertIdentities` previously swallowed every error into `return []`, so a DB failure read as "this entity has no identities" — the exact state that lets the next writer mint a duplicate. Errors now propagate. `createEntityWithIdentities` compensates by deleting the entity it had just created for those claims; a transaction is not available there because the slug-retry loop depends on surviving a failed INSERT.

A contested claim is now logged (namespaces only — an identifier here is someone's phone or email) instead of vanishing.

## Red → green

```
disable the attach branch          → 1 failed  "expected false to be true"
bypass normalization               → 3 failed  incl. unparseable-value test
drop identity_claims from deferral → 1 failed  "expected undefined to deeply equal [ { namespace: 'email', … } ]"

Two PRs in flight now, and the blocker wasn't mine.

**#2343** — the identity work. Passing so far: `base-branch-guard`, `format-lint`, `migrations`. Still pending: `typecheck`, `unit`, `integration`, `frontend`, `pi-review`.

**#2346** — https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/pull/2346, submodule pointer bump. `check-drift` failed on #2343 for a reason unrelated to my change: owletto/main had two commits merged past the pinned SHA (#632 "drop packages from skills", #633 "Behavior source chips in the composer") and nobody opened the parent bump PR. That check is required, so it fails on *every* open lobu PR until the bump lands. CI's own error message says to fix it as a separate PR, which is also what the one-branch-one-concern rule wants.

Worth flagging since it's a prod-visible side effect: **that bump carries two frontend PRs to production that aren't mine.** They were already merged on owletto/main and waiting for exactly this bump to ship, so it's the normal flow rather than me sneaking anything in — but it does mean #2346 releases someone else's composer and skills changes. I said so explicitly in the PR body.

Merge order matters here, and it's the reverse of the usual rule. Normally the owletto PR goes first, then the pointer; in this case the owletto side is already merged, so **#2346 has to merge before #2343** can go green on `check-drift`.

Monitors armed on both, emitting on failure states too rather than just success.

Confidence: high that `check-drift` is unrelated to my diff — the log names the two owletto commits and the pinned SHA explicitly, and my PR touches no submodule pointer. Unverified: whether #2343's remaining five checks pass, and the `pi-review` verdict.

Next actions:
- Merge #2346 once green, then re-run or let #2343's `check-drift` re-evaluate.
- Merge #2343 when all nine required checks report — no `--admin` past anything pending.
- Then prod verify, gated per-pod plus ancestry on the squash commits.

content.text: The reviewer's one-line characterization is imprecise but its **conclusion is correct**, and the mechanism matters. The server doesn't re-derive "whenever prompt is supplied" — it derives when `promptEdited && (prompt has chips || previously had chips)`:

input.command: cd packages/owletto && sed -n '535,555p' src/components/entity-tabs/watchers-tab/from-scratch-panel.tsx
input.description: Check the owletto side that omits sources

content.text:
Both halves confirmed. The edit path deliberately sends `sources: undefined`, and the server derives chip-only sources whenever the prompt contains a chip — so a curated non-chip source (a template prefill, or `@feed:support` with no matching token) is silently dropped on a wording-only edit.

The decisive question is whether #633 *introduced* this or it's already in prod:

input.command: git -C . log --oneline 056360959306932d199114df83c293e8cee9d2c8..005a13f0e3eb182582028e2ffa150988448589c7 -- src/components/entity-tabs/watchers-tab/from-scratch-panel.tsx | head; echo "=== diff of the sources block ==="; git -C . diff 056360959306932d199114df83c293e8cee9d2c8..005a13f0e3eb182582028e2ffa150988448589c7 -- src/components/entity-tabs/watchers-tab/from-scratch-panel.tsx | head -50
input.description: Check if #633 changed the sources omission

content.text:
I verified the blocker's direction, and the reviewer has it backwards. This matters, so here's the evidence.

**Before #633**, the edit path was:
```ts
const sources = !isEditing && prefill?.sources?.length ? prefill.sources : undefined;
```
On an edit, `!isEditing` is false — so `sources` was **always** `undefined`. Combined with the server deriving chip-only sources whenever the prompt contains a chip, *every* edit dropped curated non-chip sources.

**#633 narrows that.** It now computes explicit sources when the chip set changed, deliberately preserving stored non-chip sources, and only leaves `sources` undefined when the chip set is unchanged.

So the data loss is a **pre-existing production bug**, and #633 strictly reduces it — from "every edit" to "wording-only edits". The reviewer flagged the surviving case as though the bump introduced it and called it a blocker. The bug is real; blocking the bump on it is wrong.

That said, I'm not going to quietly merge past a failing required check on my own reading, and this is a decision about process rather than code:

**The work exists: PR #2345**, "fix(server): stop a Behavior's instruction text from authoring its sources." I found it because `make task-setup` reported the worktree already existed with that commit at HEAD — a prior session built it.

**Its design is better than what I was about to write.** I'd planned a narrow fix preserving chip-derivation while protecting non-chip sources. #2345 goes further and is right to: `lobu apply` supplies **compiled skill bodies as the prompt**, so chip-shaped prose inside a skill would silently add or remove an assignment's sources. Instruction text shouldn't be a source input at all. My narrower version would have left that hazard in place.

**Its blocker is stale.** The verdict landed 02:14:45Z; HEAD was amended 02:19:07Z, and that amendment is exactly the contract rewrite the reviewer asked for — the schema now reads "this array is the ONLY way to change them… Instruction text is never an input." ```
check-drift  → red on EVERY open lobu PR until the bump lands (incl. #2345)
#2346 (bump) → review says "wait for the server change" (= #2345)
#2345        → cannot merge, check-drift is red
```

Server-first is impossible. The bump is the only thing that clears `check-drift`, and it's this repo's documented ordering anyway. Merging it first is safe on the merits: #633 is a strict improvement on prod, narrowing the loss from every edit to wording-only edits.

So: **#2346 → #2345 → #2343.**

Confidence: high on the deadlock and the staleness — both read off commit timestamps and the actual diff, and I verified #633's direction against the pinned SHA rather than trusting either reviewer. The one thing I'd still call unresolved is whether #2346's reviewer would clear on a re-run; its blocker is about ordering, not code, so I expect it to repeat.

Next actions:
- If #2345's fresh review comes back clean, I'll need your call on #2346 again — its blocker won't change, and merging it first is now forced by the deadlock rather than chosen.
- Alternatively I fold the bump into #2345 so the frontend and server land in one commit, which dissolves both the deadlock and the reviewer's objection. That's my preference if you want this to move without an override.

content.text:
Not ready — and I'm glad I didn't merge. `pi-review` found a **real security hole I introduced**, and it's the kind worth stating plainly.

My attach path returned the resolved existing entity through `getEntity`, which only checks org scoping. It skipped the read-policy, `$member` visibility, and email-redaction gates that `handleGet` applies. So an agent allowed to create but denied read could submit a phone number it suspected existed and get that person's record back — create working as a lookup for data it can't read. My code even had a comment claiming to handle this; the comment was wrong.

**The reviewer's suggested fix would still have leaked.** It proposed gating the resolved entity. But then "denied" versus "created" *itself* answers the question — the caller learns whether that phone exists. The check has to be **type-level and before any lookup**, so the outcome can't depend on the data. Denied callers now fall through to a plain create, which is exactly what this call did before the feature existed.

Two supporting decisions: the approval-apply path passes the gate as satisfied, because it runs only under `requireHumanApprovalContext` and `manage_operations` refuses agents outright — documented at the call site rather than assumed. And the gate is injected from the tool layer, since the policy helpers are local to `manage_entity.ts` which already imports `identity-create` (importing back would cycle).

Added a regression test with create allowed and read denied, asserting a fresh entity, no attach signal, and the claim staying with its owner. Mutation-verified — disabling the gate fails it with `expected 11 not to be 11`.

**I repeated a mistake, again.** To undo that mutation I ran `git checkout --` on the file and destroyed the uncommitted fix a second time. Caught it via a `canResolveExisting` grep returning 0. From here I invert the specific edit instead of reverting files.

9/9 tests, typecheck clean, `pre-pr` green, pushed, checks and review re-running.

Confidence: high on the fix and that the oracle is genuinely closed — the gate can't see the data. Lower on my own review discipline this session; the security hole was real and I shipped it into a PR I'd called ready.

Next: merge when all nine report, then prod-verify.

content.text:
No — and I'm going to stop and recommend against merging this one on my judgment alone.

**Three review rounds, three real security findings, all mine.** The latest two:

A **cross-type leak**. My type-level gate authorized the *requested* type (`person`), but the resolved owner can be a different type — a phone claimed by a `$member`. So `create(person)` could return a member's record unredacted. Now re-checked against the owner's **actual** type, falling through to the indistinguishable create path when denied.

A **namespace squat**, which is the serious one. `normalizeRequestedIdentities` accepted *any* namespace, including `auth_user_id` — the exact claim `member-claim-predicate` uses to resolve a signed-in user to their `$member`, and it's unique per org. An agent could reserve one before real provisioning, whose `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` would then lose, silently breaking that person's member and ACL resolution.

My first attempt at that fix was a **deny-list derived from the registries, and it was unsound**. `wa_jid` slipped straight through — because `CONNECTOR_IDENTITY_MODULES` registers only github, slack and x, while WhatsApp, Instagram and LinkedIn write `wa_jid`, `ig_username` and `linkedin_slug` without appearing anywhere. There is no complete enumeration of server-written namespaces, so a deny-list cannot be made correct. It's now an allow-list of exactly `phone` and `email`. Custom namespaces are refused too — the server might own them.

41 tests green, mutation-verified (disabling the allow-list fails two), `pre-pr` clean, pushed, checks re-running.

**My recommendation: don't let me merge this.** You asked me to merge and be done, and I keep finding that the thing I called ready wasn't. The pattern is specific — every miss is in the *authorization* dimension of a feature that lets agents write identity claims into the authz substrate. Three independent holes in one small feature is a signal about the surface, not just about me. The code changes are sound and tested; what I don't trust is my own clean bill of health on it.

Concretely, I'd merge the parts that are unambiguously safe and hold the rest. But that split isn't mine to make.

There is no complete enumeration of server-written namespaces. The fix is an ALLOW-list — `phone` and `email` only, custom namespaces refused because the server may own them.

**Scope discipline.** The user asked to clear 18 approvals; that finished successfully. I then answered "what's wrong with entity_identities" and slid from diagnosis into building. ## The gap

A workspace accumulates duplicate people, and the product asks a human to merge them one by one — for a plumbing reason, not a judgement one.

Measured in prod org `buremba` on 2026-07-30, live persons:

```
persons  meta_phone  meta_email  ident_phone  ident_email
   4344         534         535           18           69
```

**1,069 identifiers sit in `entities.metadata`; 87 are real `entity_identities` claims.** Metadata has no namespace, no provenance, and — critically — no uniqueness, so nothing stops two entities holding the same number forever.

## Why it happens

Two write paths disagree, and only one of them looks before it creates.

- The connector path (`utils/entity-link-upsert.ts`) resolves incoming identifiers to their owning entity first, then attaches. That is what "upsert" means there, and it works.
- `utils/entity-management.ts::createEntity` — used by `run_sdk` and `manage_entity` — runs `INSERT INTO entities` unconditionally with a slug derived from the name. No lookup, no `ON CONFLICT`.

And `manage_entity` has **no identity parameter at all**. Verified against `origin/main`: the only `identit*` on its input side is `identity_ids` nested inside `merge_evidence`, which is merge provenance, not a write. So an agent or import can create a person and has literally no way to say "this phone identifies them" — metadata is the only slot that exists.

The 07-06 address-book import went through `run_sdk`: 541 person entities created, **3** of which got an identity row.

## The second half: uniqueness is on spelling, not meaning

`idx_entity_identities_live_unique` is `UNIQUE (organization_id, namespace, identifier) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` — the literal string. So `phone/05324764881` and `phone/905324764881` are two valid rows for one human.

This is not hypothetical. Of 18 merge approvals raised in `buremba`, 14 matched on identical digits and cleared; the remaining **4 (runs 702088, 702091, 702092, 702094) cannot be resolved deterministically at all** — the imported side stores a Turkish national-format number and the WhatsApp side stores the country-coded one.

Note the constraint here: `connector-sdk/src/identity-normalize.ts` deliberately does **not** guess country codes, and that is correct — the region knowledge lives in the importer that read the address book, not in a matcher looking at a bare string later. So this wants a canonical value supplied **at write time**, not smarter matching afterwards.

## What is NOT the problem

Worth stating, because it misdirected this investigation for a while: the 18 approvals were the resolution policy **working as designed**. `entity-resolution/policy.ts` defines `ResolutionDecision = "auto_merge" | "review"`, and every rule in `DEFAULT_PERSON_RESOLUTION_RULES` is `review` for both email and phone — because a shared phone is not proof of sameness. No uniqueness mechanism would have suppressed those reviews. `onMatch` in `x-lobu-resolution` is already the knob if auto-merge is ever wanted.

## Shape of a fix

1. Give non-connector writers an identity write path, and make `createEntity` consult the resolver the connector path already uses, so a create attaches to what exists instead of minting a duplicate.
2. Decide whether `identifier` uniqueness moves to a canonical value populated by the writer that has the region context.

## Security note — this surface needs a design review before it is built

A first attempt at (1) is open as a **draft** in #2343. Three review rounds found three independent authorization defects in it, so the agent-writable identity surface should get a deliberate security review rather than a diff-scoped one:

- Returning a resolved existing entity skips the read-policy / `$member` visibility / email-redaction gates `handleGet` applies — an agent with create-but-not-read could submit a known phone and receive that record.
- Gating on the *requested* entity type is insufficient: the resolved owner can be a different type, so `create(person)` can return a `$member`.
- Accepting arbitrary namespaces lets a caller claim `auth_user_id` — the claim `authz/member-claim-predicate` uses to resolve a signed-in user to their `$member`, unique per org. Reserving one first makes real provisioning lose its `ON CONFLICT` and silently breaks that user's member and ACL resolution.

Also worth recording: a **deny-list** of server-owned namespaces cannot be made correct. `identity/connector-identity-modules.ts` registers only github/slack/x, while WhatsApp, Instagram and LinkedIn write `wa_jid`, `ig_username` and `linkedin_slug` without appearing in any registry. An allow-list is the only sound shape.

Adjacent but distinct: #2338 (progressive multi-channel identity).
EOF

content.text:
Important correction to what I just said: the blast radius is **2 Behaviors in 1 org**, not fleet-wide. That reframes it — but it also exposes a sharper bug than the quota itself.

A 429 saying "Weekly limit exhausted, resets 2026-07-31" is a *terminal* error for the next day, yet the system retried it ~2,000 times over four days. Filing that:

input.command:
cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-burakemre-Code-lobu/c3dc213c-a275-44a5-9345-8bf68a35760f/scratchpad/issue2.md <<'EOF'
## Symptom

Measured on prod 2026-07-30 04:xx UTC. Behavior runs, last 7 days:

```
day          completed  failed  total
2026-07-30           8     218    226   (12h so far)
2026-07-29           5    1113   1119
2026-07-28           0     979    980
2026-07-27           0     288    289
2026-07-26          16      27     44
2026-07-25          17       0     18
```

Roughly **2,600 failed runs over four days**, against a normal baseline of ~16 completed/day.

Blast radius is narrow — `count(DISTINCT watcher_id) = 2`, `count(DISTINCT organization_id) = 1` — so this is not a fleet outage. Two Behaviors are hard-failing and retrying at full rate.

## Cause

199 of the last 218 failures:

```
z.ai returned an error:
429 Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted. Your limit will reset at 2026-07-31
```

## Two gaps, and the second is the sharper one

**1. No failover when an inference provider is exhausted.** A single provider's quota takes its Behaviors to zero completions. There is no fallback provider or model.

**2. A terminal provider error is retried as though it were transient.** The error names its own reset time — `2026-07-31` — and the system retried it roughly 2,000 times across four days anyway. That is the more actionable bug:

- It burns scheduler and worker capacity on work that cannot succeed until tomorrow.
- It floods `runs` with ~1,000 rows/day of identical failures, which is what made this hard to see at a glance.
- It will hammer the provider the moment quota returns, rather than easing back in.

A 429 carrying a reset timestamp should park the Behavior until that time (or trip a circuit breaker per provider+org), not re-enter the queue immediately.

## Also visible in the same window

367 failures of `Agent reply finished without calling run_sdk (client.behaviors.completeWindow) after 2 attempts` over four days, plus 55 `The agent didn't finish responding in time`. Separate from the quota issue and worth its own look — the agent producing a reply without completing the window is a distinct failure mode.

## Suggested first step

Fix (2) before (1). Honouring the reset time stops the bleeding immediately and costs far less than a provider-failover design, which needs a decision about which provider/model a workspace falls back to and who pays for it.
EOF

content.text:
Two issues filed, and the second one is the answer to your question.

**#2350 — https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/issues/2350** — is the live one. Behaviors have been failing since 27 Jul: ~2,600 failed runs over four days against a baseline of ~16 completed/day, still failing right now at 218-vs-8 in the last 12 hours. Cause is z.ai returning `429 Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted`.

I want to correct my own framing from a minute ago: I said "the Behaviors product is down" before checking the blast radius. It's **2 Behaviors in 1 org**, not fleet-wide. Narrower than I implied.

But checking that turned up a sharper bug than the quota. The 429 **names its own reset time** — 2026-07-31 — and the system retried it roughly 2,000 times anyway. A terminal error is being treated as transient. That's what buried the signal (a thousand identical rows a day), and it'll hammer the provider the moment quota returns. I'd fix that before the failover design, because it stops the bleeding today and doesn't need a decision about which provider you fall back to or who pays.

Same window also shows 367 runs where the agent replied without ever calling `completeWindow` — a distinct failure mode, noted in the issue.

**#2349 — https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/issues/2349** — the identity gap from this session's work: imports and agents can't write identity claims, so the workspace mints duplicate people it then asks you to merge. 1,069 identifiers in metadata against 87 real claims. Includes the canonical-value question and, importantly, the security review the agent-writable surface needs before #2343 gets built — with the three defects and the reason a deny-list can't work written down so nobody rediscovers them.

Confidence: high on both — every number queried from prod during this turn, not recalled.

Next actions if you want them:
- Park those 2 Behaviors manually until the 31st, which stops ~200 wasted runs/day right now without any code.
- The `completeWindow` failures probably deserve their own issue once someone's looked at one.
- #2343 stays draft pending the security review that #2349 asks for.
